reply.title: At the Highest Point of a Vertical Throw
reply.story:
When you toss a ball straight up into the air, it slows down as it climbs, stops for a brief instant at its highest point, and then speeds up on its way back down. Watching this happen, it is natural to wonder about the moment it reaches the top. Since the velocity is zero at that exact instant, does the ball also stop accelerating? 

Galileo grappled with how things change speed when falling or rising. If you measure the motion carefully, you find that the velocity changes at a steady rate the entire time the ball is in the air—even at the very top. The downward pull of gravity does not turn off just because the upward motion stops.

By tracking both the position and the velocity side by side, we can see that acceleration remains constant while velocity passes smoothly through zero. The highest point is simply where the velocity changes direction, not where the forces or acceleration disappear.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how velocity and acceleration behave when a ball is thrown straight up. At the peak, velocity is $0$, but acceleration remains constant at $-g$.
reply.instructions: Adjust the launch speed and gravity, then press play to observe how velocity and acceleration change over time.
